beginner: Kohlrabi grows best in fertile, loose, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in, and it likes steady, even moisture. The bulb stays tender and mild when the plant grows quickly without a check, so soil that holds moisture but drains well is ideal. Soil that dries out or stays soggy stresses the plant and makes the stem tough and woody.
seasoned: Kohlrabi does best in a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at even moisture, like the other cole crops. The whole game is fast, uninterrupted growth: a tender, mild swollen stem forms when the plant never checks, while drought, heat, or a stop-start water supply turns it woody, fibrous, and bitter and can crack it. Work in compost before planting and keep the bed evenly moist. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground, so keep drainage good and the pH up where it is a concern.

beginner: Kohlrabi grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a brassica soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (Iowa State gives 6 to 7; Minnesota and Utah State put the workable range at about 6.0 to 7.5). Kohlrabi tolerates roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is favored by acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral.

beginner: Kohlrabi needs decent soil and a little feeding, but not a lot. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give one feeding of a nitrogen fertilizer a few weeks later when the plants are a few inches tall. Keep the watering and feeding steady so the bulbs grow smoothly and stay tender.
seasoned: Kohlrabi is a moderate feeder that wants steady, even growth rather than a late surge. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Iowa State: 1 to 2 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting or thinning, when the plants are roughly 4 inches tall (Utah State: about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row). Keep nitrogen and water even through bulbing, since both a stall and a late flush hurt texture; avoid heavy late nitrogen, which can grow leaves at the expense of a clean bulb.

beginner: Time to feed your kohlrabi.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your kohlrabi with nitrogen as the plants establish.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then one feeding of a nitrogen fertilizer a few weeks later as the plants take off.
seasoned: A balanced base feed for steady growth: work a 10-10-10 into the bed before planting, then a single nitrogen side-dress such as 21-0-0 or blood meal about 3 to 4 weeks after planting. Keep it modest and even, since pushing the plant late grows leaves over a clean, tender bulb.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a light nitrogen feed beside the plants a few weeks later.
seasoned: Work in about 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row roughly 3 to 4 weeks after planting, banded beside the row and watered in.

beginner: Kohlrabi gets along with most vegetables. It does well next to aromatic herbs, onions and other alliums, beets, and quick leafy greens like lettuce that finish before the kohlrabi fills out. The main thing is to keep it away from its own cabbage-family relatives, which share its pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most kohlrabi companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage-family pests, low quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the kohlrabi sizes up, and beets sharing the cool-season bed. The well-grounded caution is to separate kohlrabi from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect. As University of Minnesota stresses, treat most companion claims as a starting point and watch your own results.

beginner: Onions, garlic, and chives grow tall and narrow with shallow roots, so they tuck between kohlrabi without crowding it, and their strong smell is widely used to help confuse cabbage-family pests.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, they tuck around kohlrabi without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young kohlrabi plants to use the space and shade the soil, and it is harvested long before the kohlrabi fills in. Both like the same cool weather.
seasoned: Lettuce and kohlrabi interplant well on structure and timing: lettuce is shallow and quick, kohlrabi a little slower, so the lettuce uses the open ground and light between young plants and is pulled before the kohlrabi canopies. It is an efficient cool-season space pairing, not a pest effect.

beginner: Beets are another cool-season crop that shares the bed easily with kohlrabi without competing for the same space, since beets put their energy down into the root while kohlrabi swells just above the soil.
seasoned: Beets are a traditional, low-risk cool-season neighbor for kohlrabi. They share the same season and undemanding habit, and the beet works the soil below while the kohlrabi swells at the surface, so the two coexist without much competition. A space-and-season pairing rather than a documented benefit.

beginner: Keep kohlrabi away from other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, broccoli, kale, and turnips. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them together makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting kohlrabi shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, cabbage, broccoli, kale, turnip, radish, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbageworms, loopers, flea beetles, cabbage aphids, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings. The leaves are part of why you grow kohlrabi well, and the caterpillars can also chew the bulb.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; heavy feeding sets young plants back and the larvae can score the bulb. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green, loopers move in a looping arch, and diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed.

beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants like kohlrabi and chew the leaves.
seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Kohlrabi is a primary host.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain.
seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.

beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies.
seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from planting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the folds of the leaves. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and in the leaf axils, curling and distorting the foliage and weakening young plants; heavy colonies foul the crop with honeydew.

beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants like kohlrabi and hide in the leaf folds.
seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; winged forms move in from cruciferous weeds and other brassica crops. The turnip aphid can also occur.

beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (parasitoid wasps, hoverflies, ladybugs).

beginner: Check the growing tips and leaf folds often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
seasoned: Scout growing tips and leaf axils weekly and catch infestations early. Avoid excess nitrogen, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts seedlings and slows establishment, the costly stage for a fast crop.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
seasoned: The crucifer and striped flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas; they overwinter in debris and field edges and are most damaging at the seedling stage and in spring, easing as the season warms, so fall crops face less of them.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle it.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.

beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
seasoned: Use row cover from sowing or transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, clean up weedy brassica relatives, and favor fall plantings, which see lighter pressure.

beginner: New transplants and seedlings wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
seasoned: Plants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp spring weather.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped striped eggs, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots, which later rot.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and is favored by acidic soils below about pH 6.5.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow kohlrabi or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot it.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and kill the plant. Often the most serious brassica disease in warm, wet weather.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Small, round, dark spots on the leaves, each with a yellow ring and faint target-like circles inside, that grow and run together in wet weather and turn sooty in the center.
seasoned: Small, circular, dark spots with a yellow halo and concentric rings that darken to a sooty center as spores build, enlarging and merging in wet weather. A foliar disease that weakens the plant.

beginner: Alternaria fungi that can travel on seed and survive on old plant debris, spreading in splashing water and needing wet leaves to take hold. Warm, humid weather brings it on.
seasoned: Alternaria fungi (chiefly Alternaria brassicae), which are seedborne and survive on crop debris, spreading in splashing water and needing leaf wetness to infect; warm, wet weather drives it.

beginner: Pick off the worst leaves, water at the soil in the morning so leaves dry quickly, and clean up debris. Clean seed and airflow handle most of it; a copper fungicide can help in a wet spell if started early.
seasoned: Remove badly spotted leaves, water at the base in the morning so foliage dries, and clear debris. Clean seed and airflow are the main home levers; a copper fungicide can help in a persistently wet season if started early.

beginner: Use clean seed, water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room so the leaves dry, and rotate crucifers and clear debris between plantings.
seasoned: Use clean seed, avoid overhead watering, space for airflow, and rotate crucifers and clear debris that carry the fungi between seasons.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and kills foliage. Kohlrabi's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: Pale, sunken spots dotted with tiny black specks appear on the stem and leaves, and the base of the stem darkens and rots, so the plant may topple. It often arrives on infected seed.
seasoned: Pale, sunken lesions peppered with small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) on stems and leaves, and a dark, girdling canker at the stem base that can rot the crown and lodge the plant.

beginner: A fungus that comes in on infected seed or plants and attacks the stem and leaves of cabbage-family crops. It spreads in wet weather and lingers in old plant debris.
seasoned: The fungus Phoma lingam (Leptosphaeria maculans) is chiefly seedborne and survives in brassica debris; it spreads in cool, wet weather by splashing water and infects through wounds and pores.

beginner: There's no cure, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is prevention: clean seed, rotation, and clearing away old cabbage-family debris.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Management is preventive, since the pathogen is carried on seed and in residue.

beginner: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from cabbage-family crops for a few years, and clear away old brassica plants where the fungus survives.
seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed and disease-free transplants, rotate 3 years away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Try to keep it steady, not dry-then-soaked.
seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept as even as possible; steady moisture is what keeps the bulb tender, and a dry-then-wet swing makes it woody or cracks it.

beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, a bit more in hot, dry weather.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week including rain (Iowa State and Minnesota: roughly 1 inch a week; Utah State up to 1 to 2 inches in heat or sandy soil), with the most attention while the stem is swelling.

beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage the leaf diseases kohlrabi shares with the cole crops.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; kohlrabi dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites root maggots, clubroot, and rots in cold, wet ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves and a tough, woody bulb. Letting the soil dry out is the main thing that makes kohlrabi woody, and a sudden soaking after a dry spell can crack it.
seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then woody, fibrous, strong-flavored stems; the classic kohlrabi fault is letting the bed dry out, which toughens the bulb, and a heavy soak after a dry spell can split it.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp as they grow.
seasoned: Grow the seedlings on with steady, even moisture.

beginner: Water evenly as the leaves grow before the bulb starts to swell.
seasoned: Keep even moisture as the plant leafs out ahead of the stem swelling.

beginner: Keep the water steady while the round bulb swells. If it dries out and then gets soaked, the bulb turns woody or cracks.
seasoned: Steady moisture while the stem swells is what keeps the bulb tender and crisp; a dry-then-wet swing turns it woody or cracks it open. This is the window that decides quality.

beginner: Keep watering evenly and pick kohlrabi while it is about tennis-ball size. Left too long it gets woody.
seasoned: Keep even moisture and harvest promptly at about tennis-ball size; left to oversize, kohlrabi turns woody.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the bulbs grow crisp and tender. Big swings from dry to wet are what make kohlrabi woody and cracked.
seasoned: Even, steady moisture is the whole game with kohlrabi: it keeps the swollen stem crisp, mild, and tender, and prevents the woodiness and cracking that a dry-then-wet cycle causes.

seasoned: Even moisture matters most while the stem is swelling toward harvest; this is when drought stress turns it woody and a sudden change in watering cracks it.

beginner: You can sow kohlrabi seeds right in the garden or start with young plants. For direct sowing, plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep once the soil can be worked, then thin the seedlings to about 6 to 9 inches apart. For transplants, start seeds indoors about a month before planting out, and set them in the garden a week or two before the last frost. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting. Sow again in mid-summer for a fall crop.
seasoned: Kohlrabi is grown both ways. Direct sowing is simple and common since the crop is fast: sow 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep once the soil is workable and thin to 6 to 9 inches apart. For an earlier or more uniform crop, start transplants indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and plant them out 1 to 2 weeks before the last frost, since young plants take light frost. Avoid exposing young plants to a long cold spell (more than about a week of nights below roughly 45 to 50°F), which can trigger bolting. Sow the fall crop in mid-summer. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.

beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of water. Kohlrabi needs steady, even moisture, but soil that stays soggy will rot the roots, so empty the saucer within an hour of watering.
seasoned: Do not let the pot stand in a saucer of water. Kohlrabi needs even moisture for a tender bulb, but waterlogged mix causes rot and favors clubroot; empty the saucer within an hour of watering.

beginner: Mix in a little compost to help the soil hold water evenly, which keeps kohlrabi tender.
seasoned: Use a light, loose potting mix with a handful of compost for even moisture-holding. Avoid garden soil, which compacts in a pot and can introduce the soilborne clubroot pathogen.

beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather. Kohlrabi turns woody if it dries out, so keep the moisture steady.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries out, since drying out toughens the bulb.

beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
seasoned: Container kohlrabi needs slightly more frequent feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients from the mix.

seasoned: Not applicable. Kohlrabi is grown as a single-season annual and is not held over winter in a container.

beginner: Kohlrabi is a great container crop because it is small and shallow-rooted. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep that holds 3 to 5 gallons, with drainage holes, and space the plants about 6 inches apart. Keep it watered evenly and harvest the bulbs young.
seasoned: Kohlrabi suits containers well: it is compact, shallow-rooted, and quick, so a pot 8 inches or more deep holding 3 to 5 gallons grows several plants spaced about 6 inches apart. Width matters as much as depth, since you want room for several bulbs. Keep the mix evenly moist, because pots dry fast and a checked plant turns woody, and feed lightly. Provide drainage holes and a loose potting mix.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps kohlrabi from turning woody.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits kohlrabi well, since it smooths out the steady moisture the crop needs to keep the bulb tender.

beginner: Kohlrabi has shallow roots, so a wide pot works better than a deep, narrow one. Use a container at least 8 inches deep that holds a few gallons, with drainage holes, and give each plant about 6 inches of space.
seasoned: Kohlrabi is a small, shallow-rooted plant, so a wide, fairly shallow container suits it better than a deep narrow one. Choose a pot at least 8 inches deep holding 3 to 5 gallons, and favor width so you can grow several plants spaced about 6 inches apart. Provide drainage holes and keep the mix evenly moist.

beginner: For most gardens, pick a fast standard variety like White Vienna, Purple Vienna, Grand Duke, or Kolibri, and harvest the bulbs young, about the size of a tennis ball. Purple and green types taste the same; the purple is just prettier. If you want big bulbs, grow a giant type like Kossak or Superschmelz, which stay tender even when large.
seasoned: Match the type to the slot. Fast green or purple Vienna types and hybrids like Quickstar, Grand Duke, and Kolibri are the workhorses for spring and fall, picked young at 2 to 3 inches. The purple types (Purple Vienna, Kolibri) differ from the green only in skin color, not flavor. The giant storage cultivars (Kossak, Superschmelz, Gigante) are the exception to harvest-it-small: they hold tender flesh at a much larger size and suit fall and winter storage. Where clubroot is a concern, choose resistant cultivars.

beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like cabbage, broccoli, kale, turnips, and radishes.
seasoned: Other brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, collards, turnip, radish), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.

beginner: Do not plant kohlrabi or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting a few years between them helps avoid soil diseases like clubroot.
seasoned: Rotate so brassicas do not follow brassicas for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is known, since the clubroot organism persists in soil for years. Keeping soil pH up also helps suppress it.

beginner: Plant kohlrabi so it grows in steady cool weather, not through a long cold snap or into summer heat. Setting young plants out into a hard cold spell can make them flower instead of forming a bulb, so wait for settled weather and pick bolt-resistant varieties.
seasoned: Do not rush transplants out into a long cold snap, since young kohlrabi chilled below about 45 to 50°F for a week or more is vernalized and bolts. Time the spring crop so it sizes up before summer heat, grow the fall crop into cooling weather, and choose bolt-resistant varieties such as Kolibri. Keep plants growing steadily without a check.

beginner: If young kohlrabi gets too cold for too long, or too hot, it flowers early and never makes a good bulb. Steady cool weather and good timing are the main fixes.
seasoned: Kohlrabi bolting is mainly a vernalization response: a young plant exposed to a stretch of cold runs to flower instead of swelling a stem, which is why an early spring set-out into a cold snap is the classic cause. Summer heat and long days also push it. A bolted plant will not form a usable bulb, so the fix is timing and steady growth.

beginner: Kohlrabi is a cool-season cabbage-family vegetable grown for its odd, tasty swollen stem, a round bulb, green or purple, that sits right on top of the soil with leaves sprouting from it. It is one of the fastest crops in the garden, ready in about 45 to 60 days, and grows best in the cool weather of spring and fall. The trick is simple: keep it growing steadily with even water, and pick the bulb young, about the size of a tennis ball. If you let standard kohlrabi get too big, or let it dry out or cook in summer heat, it turns woody and tough. It handles frost well, and like its cabbage cousins it gets the usual cabbage-family bugs and diseases. The bulb is crisp and mild, good raw or cooked.
seasoned: Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea, Gongylodes group) is a cool-season cole crop grown not for a head or a root but for its swollen above-ground STEM, a round, pale-green or purple bulb that sits on the soil surface topped by a rosette of leaves. It is one of the fastest brassicas, ready in about 45 to 60 days, and is grown like a quick cabbage in the cool shoulders of spring and fall. The whole craft is steady, unchecked growth and timely harvest: a tender, mild, crisp bulb forms when the plant never stalls, while drought, heat above roughly 75°F, or a stop-start water supply, or simply letting it grow too large, turns standard types woody, fibrous, and bitter. Harvest young at 2 to 3 inches, tennis-ball size; giant storage cultivars (Kossak, Superschmelz) are the exception and hold tender flesh at a much larger size. Cold-hardy and frost-tolerant, kohlrabi shares the full cabbage-family pest and disease complex.

beginner: When the seedlings have a few real leaves, thin them so each plant has about 6 to 9 inches of room. Snip the extras off at the soil instead of pulling, so you don't disturb the ones you keep. Crowded kohlrabi makes small, poor bulbs.
seasoned: Thin direct-sown kohlrabi to 6 to 9 inches apart once seedlings have 2 to 3 true leaves, snipping rather than pulling to avoid disturbing the keepers. Crowded plants compete for moisture and make small, misshapen bulbs, and crowding stress can also push them woody.
